title: Aspiration Syndromes
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Aspiration syndromes encompass a spectrum of respiratory complications from inhaled material. Clinical reasoning focuses on identifying the aspirate type, assessing severity, and tailoring urgent supportive care in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Aspiration occurs when foreign material enters the lower airways, causing inflammation, obstruction or infection. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by imaging and, where available, microbiology.
b: History of choking, coughing, or sudden respiratory distress

t.b: Shows infiltrates or atelectasis; a unilateral dense opacity suggests lobar collapse, while diffuse ground‑glass indicates aspiration pneumonitis.
Identifies bacterial colonisation in aspirated material; a positive result supports secondary infection.

sections.p: Severity is staged by respiratory compromise and oxygen requirement. In low‑resource settings, a simple clinical score based on respiratory rate, cyanosis and work of breathing is useful.
b: Severe: severe tachypnoea, nasal flaring, SpO2 <88% despite oxygen, or apnea

sections.p: The aspirate type dictates management. Common causes in East Africa include meconium in neonates, food or liquid in children, and mucus or blood in adults.
Presentation ranges from sudden coughing fits to progressive hypoxaemia. Key signs include sudden onset of wheeze, stridor, or cyanosis, often following a choking episode.
Investigations are guided by availability. In low‑resource settings, focus on bedside tests and simple imaging.

t.b: Assesses PaO2 and PaCO2; a PaO2 <60 mmHg indicates severe hypoxaemia.
Detects infiltrates, atelectasis or pneumothorax; a unilateral dense opacity suggests lobar collapse.
Identifies bacterial infection; a positive result supports antibiotic therapy.

sections.p: Urgent deterioration can lead to respiratory failure, pneumothorax, or sepsis. Watch for sudden desaturation, worsening tachypnoea, or new chest pain.
Treat the underlying cause, provide airway support, and monitor closely. In low‑resource settings, prioritize oxygen, suction, and empirical antibiotics.
b: Prepare for intubation if airway fails

sections.p: After stabilization, assess for underlying swallowing disorders or airway anomalies. Educate caregivers on safe feeding practices and early recognition of choking.
b: Schedule follow‑up chest X‑ray if persistent infiltrates

sections.p: Aspiration can mimic bronchiolitis, pneumonia, or asthma. Distinguish by history of choking, unilateral infiltrates, and response to suction.
b: Asthma – reversible wheeze, no sudden onset

sections.p: Normal chest X‑ray does not exclude aspiration; early infiltrates may be subtle. Pulse oximetry can be falsely normal if supplemental oxygen is given.
b: Oxygen therapy can mask hypoxaemia on pulse oximetry

faq.q: What is the first step if a child is choking on food?
faq.a: Clear the airway with suction or back blows; if the child cannot cough, call for emergency help.

faq.q: Which antibiotic is preferred for aspiration pneumonia in a child?
faq.a: A broad‑spectrum combination such as ampicillin plus gentamicin covers common oral flora.

faq.q: How can you differentiate aspiration pneumonia from bronchiolitis?
faq.a: Aspiration often follows choking, shows unilateral infiltrates, and improves with suction; bronchiolitis is viral, bilateral, and improves with supportive care.

exam: What is the most urgent intervention in a child with sudden choking and cyanosis? — Clear airway with suction or Heimlich manoeuvre, then call for help.
How would you differentiate aspiration pneumonitis from bacterial pneumonia on chest X‑ray? — Look for unilateral dense opacity or atelectasis versus bilateral infiltrates.
Why is empirical antibiotic therapy started in aspiration pneumonia even if the aspirate is sterile? — To cover potential bacterial colonisation from oral flora.
What red flag would prompt immediate intubation in a patient with aspiration? — Sudden drop in SpO2 below 88% despite oxygen, or worsening respiratory effort.
Which low‑resource investigation can help confirm aspiration if a chest X‑ray is unavailable? — Pulse oximetry and clinical observation of cough and wheeze.
Why is bronchodilator therapy considered in aspiration with wheeze? — It relieves bronchospasm caused by inflammatory mediators in the airway.
When is a chest X‑ray unnecessary in a suspected aspiration case? — If the child is stable, SpO2 >92% on room air, and no signs of severe distress.
